A race occurs when goroutines access shared data without coordination and at least one writes to it. Deadlock means tasks are stuck waiting; the race detector does not detect every deadlock.

Choosing a model starts with the problem: what inputs does it take, and which output do you need? A larger model is not necessarily better for learning, and loading it alone may require more memory than the device has.
The model record should include its revision, license and limitations. Memory requirements extend beyond weights; input length, activations, batch size and the optimizer also matter.
Define a small objective
For example, choose short-text classification or a limited rewriting task. Define the data type, language and success metric before choosing a model.
Review the model card
Choose a small model and dataset; record their exact names, revisions, licenses, usage limits and input/output formats from their official pages.
Try a baseline run
Run a few examples with a small batch on the CPU or an available device. Measure RAM/VRAM and time; describe a Colab route as executed only if you have actually set it up and run it.
Prepare a model selection record including baseline execution results.
Three short synthetic texts with a specified language and length; the actual device available to you.
Record the model name, license, revision, settings and real sample outputs, along with memory limits.
If the model does not fit, reduce model size and sequence length first; do not report the roadmap's hypothetical GPU as your own hardware.
Downloadable weights do not imply permission for every commercial use or dataset.
An experiment plan written before execution makes comparisons interpretable. If data, seed, metrics or settings change midway, a result difference cannot be attributed to a single factor.
A checkpoint is more than a weights file; reproducing it also requires the base model, tokenizer, settings, package versions and data preparation method.
Fix the data and metric
Record train/validation/test sample IDs or files separately. Define a suitable metric and an untrained baseline; do not use test data for intermediate decisions.
Write down the budget
Choose epochs, batch size, learning rate, sequence length and full/LoRA training according to your actual device. Plan a short run of a few batches first.
Define stopping and saving
Specify checkpoint names, evaluation intervals and a stopping condition. Keep the configuration file and seed with the report and record memory usage.
Create an experiment plan and baseline before training.
A small dataset with a fixed split; your available memory and maximum execution time.
Another person can identify the data, model, metric and settings to run from the plan alone.
Do not change two or more settings at once; run the fixed baseline first.
Repeatedly choosing the best epoch using test data makes final evaluation overly optimistic.
Training loss and quality on new data are different things. If training improves while validation worsens, more training may increase memorization or overfitting.
An interim report should separate observation from interpretation. Validation loss increased is an observation; the learning rate is too high is a hypothesis that needs another experiment.
Compare epoch reports
For each epoch, tabulate training loss, validation loss or another suitable metric, time and settings. Record model mistakes without cherry-picking examples.
Base decisions on the metric
Compare results with the baseline and the previous plan's stopping condition. If validation worsens, keep an appropriate checkpoint; falling training loss alone does not justify continuing.
Choose one next factor
To investigate improvement, change just one of data, learning rate, epoch count or regularization. Write down the hypothesis and its confirmation metric before the next run.
Record a decision to continue or stop, backed by a table of evidence.
Do not call epoch three the best merely because training loss is lower; explain checkpoint selection and the limits of the result.
When interpreting numbers, also verify that the validation set and calculation method are unchanged.
An attractive chart without sample counts and settings is not a reproducible result.

Create a final report with a small reproduction command and a table of devices.

Readers can tell what actually ran, the quality result and which parts were not executed because of limitations.
